observation_summary: The StringEscapeUtils.escapeHtml method incorrectly processes high-unicode characters (those represented as surrogate pairs in Java) by treating them as two separate characters instead of a single code point, resulting in incorrect HTML entity output.
hypothesis: The original implementation used charAt(i) which only retrieves 16-bit char values. For characters outside the Basic Multilingual Plane (BMP), this splits the surrogate pair. The fix requires using Character.codePointAt(str, i) to correctly identify the full 32-bit Unicode code point and adjusting the loop index accordingly.
prediction: The code will be updated to use Character.codePointAt(str, i) instead of charAt(i), and a new conditional branch will be added to handle the 32-bit code points by incrementing the loop index to skip the second half of the surrogate pair.
experiment_rationale: The diff shows a change from charAt(i) to Character.codePointAt(str, i) and the addition of logic to handle code points >= 0x010000, confirming that the procedural logic for character iteration and identification was flawed.
reasoning_summary: The defect is a procedural error in how the string is iterated and how characters are identified. The original algorithm assumed all characters fit into a single 16-bit char, which is incorrect for high-unicode characters. The fix involves changing the iteration strategy (using code points) and the computational logic for handling these specific characters, which fits the definition of Algorithm/Method.
evidence_used: The diff shows the replacement of 'char c = str.charAt(i)' with 'int c = Character.codePointAt(str, i)'.
The diff shows the addition of a conditional block to handle 'c >= 0x010000' and incrementing 'i'.
The bug report states that characters represented as 2 characters internally are incorrectly converted.

alternative_types.why_not_primary: While a check was added, the core issue is the incorrect procedural approach to character iteration and identification, not just a missing guard.
This is a local procedural fix within an existing method, not a design-level capability gap.
